prompt: What is a **compound**?

options.text: Two or more different elements chemically joined together
Two or more substances mixed together but not joined
A substance made of only one type of atom
Any substance that dissolves in water

feedback.b: That's a mixture. In a compound the elements are chemically bonded.
feedback.d: Some compounds dissolve and some don't. Dissolving isn't what makes something a compound.

hints: Water is a compound of hydrogen and oxygen.
solution: A compound is made of **two or more different elements chemically joined** in a fixed ratio. For example, water (H₂O) always has 2 hydrogen atoms joined to 1 oxygen atom.

prompt: In a solution, what is the name of the substance that **dissolves**, such as sugar in a cup of tea?
hints: The liquid that does the dissolving is the solvent.
solution: The substance that dissolves is the **solute**. The liquid it dissolves in is the solvent, and together they make a solution.

prompt: How many atoms altogether are in one molecule of carbon dioxide, CO₂?
hints: No number after a symbol means 1 atom.
solution: CO₂ has 1 carbon atom and 2 oxygen atoms: $1 + 2 = 3$ atoms.

prompt: Which separation method uses filter paper to separate an insoluble solid, like sand, from a liquid?
hints: The name comes from the paper you use.
solution: **Filtration.** The liquid passes through the filter paper (the filtrate), and the sand is left behind on the paper (the residue).

prompt: Match each separation method to the job it does best.

right.text: Get salt crystals from salt water
Get pure water from sea water
Separate the dyes in a felt-tip pen's ink
Separate iron filings from sulfur powder

hints: Evaporation keeps the solid; distillation keeps the liquid.
solution: Filtration: sand from water. Evaporation: salt from salt water (the water is lost). Distillation: pure water from sea water (the water is collected). Chromatography: dyes in ink. Magnet: iron from sulfur.

prompt: Which box shows a **compound**?

options.text: Box A
Box B
Box C
Box D

feedback.a: Box A has only one kind of atom, so it's an element.
feedback.b: Box B has molecules, but each one is made of the same kind of atom, so it's an element.
feedback.d: Box D has two different kinds of particle that aren't joined to each other, so it's a mixture.

hints: A compound's particles each contain different kinds of atom joined together.
In a compound, every particle is the same.
solution: **Box C.** Every particle is the same, and each one is made of two different kinds of atom joined together, so it's a compound (it looks like water, H₂O).

options.text: Box A
Box B
Box C
Box D

feedback.a: Box A has only one kind of particle.
feedback.b: Box B has only one kind of particle (a molecule of an element).
feedback.c: Box C has two kinds of atom, but they are joined, and all the particles are the same. That makes it a compound.

hints: A mixture has more than one kind of particle in it.
solution: **Box D.** It contains two different kinds of particle (light pairs and single dark atoms) that aren't joined to each other, so it's a mixture of two elements.

prompt: Which boxes show an **element**? Select **all** that apply.

options.text: Box A
Box B
Box C
Box D

hints: An element has only one kind of atom, but those atoms can be single or joined in molecules.
solution: **Boxes A and B.** Each contains only one kind of atom. In A the atoms are separate (like helium), and in B they are joined in pairs (like oxygen, O₂). Molecules of an element are still an element.

prompt: Sugar dissolves in water to make a sugar solution. The sugar is the [[a]], the water is the [[b]], and we say sugar is [[c]] in water.
hints: The solute dissolves in the solvent.
solution: Sugar is the **solute** (it dissolves), water is the **solvent** (it does the dissolving), and sugar is **soluble** in water.

prompt: In chemistry, which of these is a **pure substance**?

options.text: Distilled water
Sea water
Air
100% pure orange juice

feedback.b: Sea water is a mixture of water and dissolved salts.
feedback.c: Air is a mixture of nitrogen, oxygen, argon, carbon dioxide and other gases.
feedback.d: In everyday language 'pure' means nothing added, but in chemistry orange juice is a mixture of water, sugars, acids and more.

hints: In chemistry, 'pure' means containing only one substance.
solution: **Distilled water** contains only water molecules, so it's a pure substance. The others are all mixtures.

prompt: Co has a capital C and a lower-case o, so it is the element [[a]]. CO has two capital letters, so it is a [[b]] of carbon and oxygen.
hints: Every capital letter starts a new element symbol.
solution: Co is the element **cobalt**. CO has two capitals, so it is two elements, carbon and oxygen, joined together: a **compound** (carbon monoxide).

prompt: A student dissolves 15 g of salt in 200 g of water. What is the mass of the salt solution?
hints: When salt dissolves, does it disappear, or is it still there?
solution: The salt hasn't disappeared. Its particles have spread out between the water particles. Mass of solution = 15 + 200 = **215 g**.

prompt: Select **all** the compounds.

options.text: H₂O
CO₂
O₂
NaCl
He
CH₄
N₂

hints: Count the different symbols (capital letters) in each formula.
O₂ is a molecule, but is it made of different elements?
solution: A compound contains **two or more different elements**: H₂O, CO₂, NaCl and CH₄. O₂ and N₂ are molecules made of only one element, and He is a single atom, so they are elements.

prompt: Put the steps for distilling sea water in order.

items.text: Heat the sea water in a flask
The water boils and turns into water vapour
The vapour passes into a condenser cooled by cold water
The vapour condenses back into liquid water
Pure water drips into a beaker

hints: Distillation is evaporation (boiling) followed by condensation.
solution: Heat → the water boils → the vapour enters the cold condenser → it condenses → pure water is collected. The salt stays behind in the flask because it doesn't boil at 100 °C.

prompt: In paper chromatography, why is the start line drawn in **pencil** rather than pen?

options.text: Pencil won't dissolve in the solvent, but pen ink might run up the paper
Pencil is easier to rub out if you make a mistake
Pen ink would stop the solvent moving up the paper
Pencil makes the dyes travel faster

feedback.b: That's true, but it isn't the scientific reason.
feedback.c: The solvent would still move. The problem is that pen ink could dissolve and mix with your results.
feedback.d: The pencil line doesn't change how fast the dyes travel.

hints: What would happen to a line drawn in ink when the solvent reached it?
solution: Pencil (graphite) **doesn't dissolve** in the solvent. A pen line could dissolve and separate into its own dyes, which would mix with the dyes you are testing.

prompt: Which statement best describes the particles in solid sodium chloride (table salt)?

options.text: Positive sodium ions and negative chloride ions in a regular, repeating lattice
Separate NaCl molecules, each made of one sodium atom and one chlorine atom
Sodium atoms and chlorine atoms mixed together but not joined
Sodium ions and chloride ions moving freely, like a gas

feedback.b: Sodium chloride doesn't form separate molecules. It forms a giant lattice, and the formula shows the 1 : 1 ratio of ions.
feedback.c: Sodium chloride is a compound, not a mixture. The sodium and chlorine are chemically joined.
feedback.d: In the solid the ions are held in fixed positions. They can move only when it is melted or dissolved.

hints: Sodium chloride is made from a metal and a non-metal, so it is ionic.
solution: Sodium chloride is an **ionic lattice**: positive sodium ions and negative chloride ions packed in a huge, regular 3D pattern, held together by the strong attraction between opposite charges.

prompt: Iron filings and sulfur powder stirred together can be separated using a [[a]]. When the mixture is heated, they react to form iron sulfide, a new [[b]], and the iron can no longer be pulled out this way.
hints: Iron is magnetic; sulfur isn't.
When elements react and become chemically joined, what do they make?
solution: A **magnet** separates the mixture, because the iron isn't joined to the sulfur. After heating, the iron and sulfur are chemically joined in a **compound**, iron sulfide, so the magnet can't pull the iron out any more.

prompt: Explain the difference between a **mixture** and a **compound**.
modelAnswer: In a compound, two or more different elements are chemically joined (bonded) in a fixed ratio, and it can only be split up by a chemical reaction. In a mixture, the substances are not chemically joined, they can be in any amounts, each keeps its own properties, and they can be separated by physical methods such as filtering or using a magnet.

rubric.criterion: Compound: elements are chemically joined in a fixed ratio (separated only by a chemical reaction)
Mixture: substances are not chemically joined and can be separated by physical methods (or can be in any amounts)

hints: Think about whether the parts are joined, and how you could separate them.
solution: Compound: chemically joined, fixed ratio, needs a chemical reaction to separate. Mixture: not joined, any amounts, separated physically (e.g. filtering, evaporating, a magnet).

prompt: Sodium is a soft, very reactive metal. Chlorine is a poisonous yellow-green gas. Yet sodium chloride is the salt we sprinkle on chips. What does this show about compounds?

options.text: A compound can have very different properties from the elements it is made from
A compound always has the properties of its most reactive element
Sodium chloride is really a mixture of sodium and chlorine
Poisonous elements always make poisonous compounds

feedback.b: Salt doesn't behave like sodium at all. It doesn't fizz in water.
feedback.c: If it were a mixture, it would still have the properties of sodium and chlorine.
feedback.d: Sodium chloride is a clear example where that isn't true.

hints: Does table salt behave like sodium metal or chlorine gas?
solution: When elements are chemically joined, they make a **new substance with new properties**. Sodium chloride behaves nothing like sodium or chlorine. This is a key difference between a compound and a mixture.

prompt: At 20 °C, a maximum of 36 g of salt will dissolve in 100 g of water. What is the maximum mass of salt that will dissolve in 250 g of water at 20 °C?
hints: 250 g of water is how many times as much as 100 g?
Multiply 36 g by that number.
solution: 250 g of water is $250 \div 100 = 2.5$ times as much water, so it can dissolve 2.5 times as much salt: $36 \times 2.5 = $ **90 g**.

prompt: Describe how you could get pure, dry salt crystals from a mixture of salt and sand.
modelAnswer: 1. Add water to the mixture and stir. The salt dissolves, but the sand doesn't. 2. Filter the mixture. The sand stays on the filter paper as the residue, and the salt solution passes through as the filtrate. 3. Evaporate the water from the salt solution by heating it gently, or by leaving it in a warm place, until salt crystals are left behind.

rubric.criterion: Add water and stir so the salt dissolves (the sand doesn't)
Filter to remove the sand: the sand stays on the filter paper and the salt solution passes through
Evaporate the water from the solution to leave salt crystals

hints: One of the two substances dissolves in water and the other doesn't.
You need three steps: dissolve, separate the sand, then get the salt back.
solution: Dissolve (add water and stir), then filter (the sand is caught by the paper), then evaporate (the water leaves, and the salt crystals stay).

prompt: Substance Y is a white crystalline solid. It melts at 801 °C. It doesn't conduct electricity as a solid, but it does when it is melted or dissolved in water. What type of substance is Y most likely to be?

options.text: An ionic compound (a salt) with a lattice structure
A molecular substance, like sugar
A metal
A noble gas

feedback.b: Molecular substances have low melting points and don't conduct, even when melted.
feedback.c: Metals conduct electricity when they are solid.
feedback.d: Noble gases are gases at room temperature.

hints: A high melting point means strong forces hold the particles together.
Conducting only when melted or dissolved means charged particles are free to move only then.
solution: A high melting point and conducting only when melted or dissolved are signs of an **ionic lattice**. When it melts or dissolves, the ions can move and carry charge. (Y is sodium chloride.)

prompt: Two inks are tested with paper chromatography on the same paper, using the same solvent. Ink X separates into a blue spot and a red spot. Ink Y makes a single blue spot that travels exactly as far as ink X's blue spot. Select **all** the conclusions that are supported.

options.text: Ink X is a mixture
Inks X and Y probably contain the same blue dye
Ink Y could be a single dye
Ink Y contains the red dye
Ink X is a pure substance

hints: How many substances does each spot represent?
Under the same conditions, the same dye travels the same distance.
solution: Ink X splits into two spots, so it is a **mixture** of at least two dyes. The blue spots travel the same distance under the same conditions, so they are **probably the same dye**. Ink Y gives only one spot, so it **could be a single dye**. Ink Y has no red spot, so it doesn't contain the red dye.

prompt: Which observation is the best evidence that air is a **mixture** rather than a compound?

options.text: The amount of water vapour in air changes from day to day and place to place
Air is invisible
Air contains oxygen, which we need to breathe
Air can be squashed into a smaller space

feedback.b: Many substances are invisible, including some pure ones. This doesn't tell you anything about mixtures.
feedback.c: This is true, but it doesn't show whether the gases are joined or not.
feedback.d: All gases can be squashed. That's because the particles are far apart, not because air is a mixture.

hints: A compound always has a fixed ratio of elements. Can the make-up of a mixture change?
solution: A compound always has a **fixed** composition, but the parts of a mixture can be present in any amounts. Because the amount of water vapour in air **varies**, air must be a mixture.

prompt: Ethanol boils at 78 °C and water boils at 100 °C. Explain how distillation could separate ethanol from a mixture of ethanol and water.
modelAnswer: Heat the mixture gently so its temperature is about 78 °C, above ethanol's boiling point but below water's. The ethanol boils (evaporates) first, because it has the lower boiling point, while most of the water stays as a liquid in the flask. The ethanol vapour passes into a cold condenser, where it cools and condenses back into liquid ethanol, which is collected in a separate container. Some water also evaporates, so the ethanol collected isn't completely pure.

rubric.criterion: Heat the mixture to about 78 °C (above ethanol's boiling point but below water's)
Ethanol boils or evaporates first because of its lower boiling point, while most of the water stays liquid
The ethanol vapour is cooled in a condenser, condenses back to a liquid and is collected separately

hints: Which liquid turns into a gas first as the mixture heats up?
How do you turn the vapour back into a liquid?
solution: Heat to about 78 °C, so the ethanol boils off first (it has the lower boiling point). Its vapour condenses in the cold condenser and is collected. Because the boiling points are close, a little water comes over too. That's why repeated (fractional) distillation is used in industry.

prompt: How many oxygen atoms are shown in the formula of aluminium sulfate, Al₂(SO₄)₃?
hints: The 3 after the bracket multiplies everything inside the bracket.
How many oxygen atoms are in one SO₄?
solution: Inside the bracket, SO₄ has 4 oxygen atoms. The bracket is multiplied by 3, so there are $4 \times 3 = 12$ oxygen atoms. (In total: Al 2, S 3, O 12.)

prompt: Explain why the dyes in the lolly coating separate into different spots.
modelAnswer: The water (the solvent) soaks up the paper and dissolves the dyes, carrying them upwards. Each dye is different: some dissolve better in the water and are held less strongly by the paper, so they travel further, while others are held more strongly by the paper and travel a shorter distance. Because each dye moves a different distance, the mixture separates into separate spots.

rubric.criterion: The water (solvent) moves up the paper, dissolving the dyes and carrying them with it
Different dyes have different solubility in the water or are attracted to the paper by different amounts
So the dyes travel different distances (at different speeds) and end up as separate spots

hints: What carries the dyes up the paper?
Why would one dye travel further than another?
solution: Solvent carries the dyes up; each dye has its own solubility and attraction to the paper, so each travels a different distance, and the mixture separates.

stem: At Lake Grassmere in Marlborough, salt is made from sea water. Sea water is let into a series of large, shallow ponds, where the Sun and the wind slowly evaporate the water until salt crystals form.
prompt: Is sea water a pure substance?

options.text: No, it is a mixture: water with salts dissolved in it
Yes, because it looks clear and the same all the way through
Yes, because it is mostly water
No, it is a compound of salt and water joined together

feedback.b: Many solutions look clear and even. Looking the same all through does not mean only one substance is there.
feedback.c: Being mostly water is not enough. A pure substance contains only one substance.
feedback.d: The salt and water are not chemically joined. The salt can be separated just by evaporating the water.

hints: A pure substance contains only one element or one compound.
solution: Sea water is a **mixture** (a solution) of water with salts, mainly sodium chloride, dissolved in it. The salts can be separated from the water by evaporation, a physical method.

stem: At Lake Grassmere in Marlborough, salt is made from sea water. Sea water is let into a series of large, shallow ponds, where the Sun and the wind slowly evaporate the water until salt crystals form.
prompt: Sea water contains about 35 g of dissolved salts in every 1 kg of sea water. What mass of salts could be obtained by evaporating 20 kg of sea water? Give your answer in **grams**.
hints: Each kilogram gives 35 g of salts.
Multiply by the number of kilograms.
solution: 20 kg × 35 g per kg = **700 g** of salts.

stem: At Lake Grassmere in Marlborough, salt is made from sea water. Sea water is let into a series of large, shallow ponds, where the Sun and the wind slowly evaporate the water until salt crystals form.
prompt: Explain why **shallow** ponds in a **sunny, windy** place are a good way to get the salt out of sea water.
modelAnswer: Evaporation happens at the surface of a liquid. Shallow ponds spread the water out so it has a large surface area, so more water particles can escape and it evaporates faster. Sunshine heats the water, giving the particles more energy so more of them escape, and the wind carries the water vapour away from the surface so evaporation keeps going.

rubric.criterion: Evaporation happens at the surface, so shallow ponds (a large surface area) let the water evaporate faster
The Sun heats the water (particles gain energy) and/or the wind carries water vapour away, which speeds up evaporation

hints: Where does evaporation happen?
Think about what makes washing dry quickly on a clothesline.
solution: Large surface area (shallow), warmth from the Sun and wind all speed up evaporation, leaving the salt behind.

options.text: Hydrogen sulfide, H₂S
Calcium carbonate, CaCO₃
Sodium hydrogen carbonate, NaHCO₃
Citric acid, C₆H₈O₇
Oxygen, O₂

hints: A compound contains two or more **different** elements chemically joined.
How many different elements are in O₂?
solution: H₂S, CaCO₃, NaHCO₃ and C₆H₈O₇ each contain more than one element, so they are **compounds**. O₂ has two atoms joined together, but both are oxygen, so it is an **element**.

prompt: During filtration, what is the name of the liquid that passes through the filter paper?
hints: The solid left on the filter paper is called the residue.
solution: The liquid that passes through is the **filtrate**. The solid left behind on the filter paper is the residue.

prompt: Salt dissolves in water, so it is [[a]]. Sand does not dissolve in water, so it is [[b]]. A solution that cannot dissolve any more salt is [[c]].
hints: "In-" at the start of a word often means "not".
solution: Salt is **soluble**, sand is **insoluble**, and a solution that can't dissolve any more solute is **saturated**.

prompt: Brass, used for door handles and trumpets, is made by melting copper and zinc together and letting them set. Brass can be made with different amounts of zinc. What type of substance is brass?

options.text: A mixture of metals (an alloy)
A compound of copper and zinc
A new element
A pure substance

feedback.b: In a compound the elements are chemically joined in a fixed ratio. Brass can contain different amounts of zinc, so it is not a compound.
feedback.c: An element contains only one type of atom. Brass contains copper atoms and zinc atoms.
feedback.d: Brass contains two different substances, copper and zinc, so it is not pure.

hints: Are the amounts of copper and zinc fixed?
solution: Brass is an **alloy**, a mixture of metals. The copper and zinc are not chemically joined, which is why the proportions can vary. Steel (iron with a little carbon) is another alloy.

prompt: Match each term to its description.

right.text: Made of only one type of atom
Two or more elements chemically joined in a fixed ratio
Two or more substances together but not chemically joined
A mixture where one substance is dissolved evenly in another
Contains only one element or only one compound

hints: A solution is a special kind of mixture.
solution: Element: one type of atom. Compound: elements chemically joined in a fixed ratio. Mixture: substances together but not joined. Solution: one substance dissolved evenly in another. Pure substance: only one element or one compound.

prompt: Select **all** the **mixtures**.

options.text: Sea water
Air
Milk
Steel
Distilled water
Oxygen
Sodium chloride
Carbon dioxide

hints: Steel is iron with a little carbon added. Milk contains water, fats, proteins and sugar.
solution: **Sea water, air, milk and steel** are mixtures: each contains several substances that are not chemically joined. Distilled water and carbon dioxide are compounds, oxygen is an element, and sodium chloride is a compound. They are all pure substances.

prompt: Sugar dissolves faster in hot tea than in iced tea. Why?

options.text: The particles in hot tea move faster, so they hit the sugar more often and its particles spread out more quickly
The heat melts the sugar first, and the melted sugar then mixes into the tea quickly
The water particles in hot tea are bigger, so each one can carry away more sugar
Cold water cannot dissolve sugar at all, so only the hot tea dissolves it

feedback.b: Tea is far below the melting point of sugar (about 186 °C). The sugar dissolves; it doesn't melt.
feedback.c: Particles do not change size when they are heated. They just move faster.
feedback.d: Sugar does dissolve in cold water, just more slowly.

hints: How does temperature affect the movement of particles?
solution: In hot tea the water particles have more energy and move **faster**. They collide with the sugar more often and with more energy, so the sugar particles break away and spread out more quickly. Stirring and using smaller sugar crystals also speed up dissolving.

prompt: Put the steps in order to separate a mixture of iron filings, salt and sand, so that you end up with all three separately.

items.text: While the mixture is dry, use a magnet to pull out the iron filings
Add water to the sand and salt, and stir so the salt dissolves
Filter the mixture: the sand stays on the filter paper
Evaporate the water from the filtrate to leave the salt

hints: Which substance is magnetic?
You can only filter out the sand once the salt has dissolved.
solution: Magnet first (removes the iron while the mixture is dry) → add water to dissolve the salt → filter to trap the sand → evaporate the filtrate to get the salt.

prompt: You want to separate **pure water** from some blue ink and **collect the water**. Which method should you use?

options.text: Distillation
Filtration
Evaporation in an open dish
Chromatography

feedback.b: The dyes are dissolved in the water, so they pass straight through the filter paper with it.
feedback.c: Evaporation leaves the dye behind, but the water escapes into the air, so you can't collect it.
feedback.d: Chromatography separates the different dyes in the ink, but it doesn't give you the water.

hints: You need to turn the water into a gas and then catch it again.
solution: **Distillation**: the water is boiled off, the vapour is cooled in a condenser and turns back into pure liquid water, which is collected. The ink dyes stay behind in the flask.

prompt: A student has some clear, colourless liquid that she thinks is pure water. Which test would best show whether it is pure?

options.text: Check that it boils at exactly 100 °C (at sea level) and freezes at exactly 0 °C
Check that it looks clear and colourless, with nothing floating in it
Pour it through filter paper and see whether anything is left on the paper
Taste a little to check that it has no flavour at all

feedback.b: Many solutions, such as salt water and sugar water, look clear and colourless.
feedback.c: Dissolved substances pass straight through filter paper, so this can't show that nothing is dissolved.
feedback.d: Never taste anything in a lab. Also, some dissolved substances have no taste.

hints: Pure substances have fixed melting and boiling points. Dissolved impurities change them.
solution: A pure substance has a **fixed boiling point and melting point**. Pure water boils at exactly 100 °C (at sea level) and freezes at exactly 0 °C. Dissolved impurities raise the boiling point and lower the freezing point.

prompt: In a chromatography experiment, a student sets up the paper so that the spots of ink are **below** the water level in the beaker. What will happen?

options.text: The dyes will dissolve into the water in the beaker instead of moving up the paper
The dyes will travel up the paper faster and separate even better
Nothing will change, because the water level does not matter
The water will not soak up the paper at all

feedback.b: The dyes are washed off the paper into the beaker, so they don't get carried up the paper to separate.
feedback.c: The water level matters: the spots must be above it so the water reaches them by soaking up the paper.
feedback.d: The paper still soaks up water, but the dyes have already been washed off into the beaker.

hints: What does water do to the dyes when they touch it directly?
solution: If the spots are under the water, the dyes **dissolve into the water in the beaker** and are washed away, so there is little or nothing to separate. The start line must always be above the solvent level.

prompt: Which statements about **water**, H₂O, are correct? Select **all** that apply.

options.text: It is made of hydrogen and oxygen atoms chemically joined together
Every water molecule has two hydrogen atoms and one oxygen atom
Its properties are very different from those of hydrogen and oxygen
It can be separated into hydrogen and oxygen by boiling it
It is a mixture of hydrogen gas and oxygen gas
The amount of oxygen in water varies from sample to sample

hints: Water is a compound. What is true of every compound?
What is steam made of?
solution: Water is a **compound**: hydrogen and oxygen chemically joined, always in the ratio 2 H : 1 O, with properties unlike either element (hydrogen burns and oxygen helps things burn, but water puts fires out). Boiling only turns water into steam, which is still H₂O; splitting water needs a chemical reaction.

prompt: Describe how you could get pure drinking water from a sample of muddy, salty water. Explain why each step is needed.
modelAnswer: First filter the water. The mud is made of insoluble particles, so it is trapped on the filter paper. The salt is dissolved, so it passes through the filter paper with the water, which means filtering alone does not make the water pure. Then distil the filtrate: heat it until the water boils, cool the water vapour in a condenser so it condenses back into liquid, and collect this pure water. The salt stays behind in the flask.

rubric.criterion: Filter to remove the mud (insoluble particles stay on the filter paper)
Explains that the salt is dissolved, so it passes through the filter and another step is needed
Distil: boil the water, condense the vapour in a condenser and collect the pure water (salt stays behind)

hints: The mud and the salt need different methods.
Which method lets you collect the water rather than lose it to the air?
solution: Filter (removes insoluble mud) → distil the filtrate (boil, condense and collect the water; the dissolved salt is left behind).

prompt: Sam says, "Salt water is a compound, because the salt and the water are joined together." Explain why Sam is wrong. Give **two** pieces of evidence.
modelAnswer: Salt water is a mixture (a solution), not a compound, because the salt and water are not chemically joined. Evidence 1: the salt can be got back just by evaporating the water, which is a physical method; separating a compound needs a chemical reaction. Evidence 2: you can dissolve different amounts of salt in the same amount of water, but a compound always has a fixed ratio of elements. (Also, the salt and water keep their own properties: the water still tastes salty.)

rubric.criterion: Salt water is a mixture (solution): the salt and water are not chemically joined
Evidence: the salt can be separated by a physical method such as evaporation
Second piece of evidence: the amount of salt can vary (no fixed ratio), or the salt and water keep their own properties

hints: How can you get the salt back out?
Can you make salt water stronger or weaker?
solution: It is a mixture. Evaporation separates it (physical method), and the proportions can vary; a compound has a fixed ratio and needs a chemical reaction to separate it.

prompt: At 60 °C, up to 110 g of potassium nitrate will dissolve in 100 g of water. At 20 °C, only 32 g will dissolve. A saturated solution of potassium nitrate in 100 g of water at 60 °C is cooled to 20 °C. What mass of potassium nitrate crystals forms?
hints: How much is dissolved at 60 °C? How much can stay dissolved at 20 °C?
The rest comes out of the solution as crystals.
solution: At 60 °C the saturated solution holds 110 g. At 20 °C only 32 g can stay dissolved, so 110 − 32 = **78 g** crystallises out.

prompt: A mixture of ethanol (boils at 78 °C) and water (boils at 100 °C) is distilled. The liquid collected at around 78 °C is mostly ethanol, but tests show it still contains a little water. Why?

options.text: Some water evaporates even below its boiling point, so a little is carried over with the ethanol
Ethanol and water are chemically joined, so they can never be separated
The thermometer must be faulty, because ethanol always distils on its own at 78 °C
Some of the ethanol turns into water when it is heated

feedback.b: They are a mixture, not a compound. Distillation separates most of the ethanol from the water.
feedback.c: The thermometer is fine. The problem is that water also evaporates at 78 °C, just more slowly.
feedback.d: Heating ethanol in distillation is a physical change. It doesn't turn into a different substance.

hints: Does a liquid have to reach its boiling point before any of it can evaporate?
solution: Evaporation happens at **any** temperature, not just at the boiling point. At 78 °C some water particles also have enough energy to escape, so a little water vapour is carried over and condenses with the ethanol. That is why simple distillation can't make completely pure ethanol from this mixture.

prompt: Sodium chloride (table salt) melts at 801 °C, but sugar melts at only about 186 °C. Use ideas about **ionic lattices** and **molecules** to explain this difference.
modelAnswer: Sodium chloride is an ionic compound. It forms a giant lattice: a huge, regular arrangement of positive sodium ions and negative chloride ions. Every ion is strongly attracted to the oppositely charged ions around it, all through the lattice, so a lot of energy (a very high temperature) is needed to break the lattice apart and melt it. Sugar is made of separate molecules. The forces holding one sugar molecule to the next are much weaker, so much less energy is needed to separate the molecules, and sugar melts at a much lower temperature.

rubric.criterion: Sodium chloride is a giant lattice of positive sodium ions and negative chloride ions
Strong attractions between oppositely charged ions all through the lattice need a lot of energy (high temperature) to overcome
Sugar is made of separate molecules with weak forces between them, so less energy is needed and it melts at a lower temperature

hints: What holds the particles together in each substance?
Melting means separating the particles enough that they can move past each other.
solution: Salt: a lattice of oppositely charged ions with strong attractions throughout, so a high melting point. Sugar: separate molecules with weak forces between them, so a lower melting point.
